faq.answer: It does not establish low self-esteem. The facet includes self-evaluation content but is not an assessment of overall worth. Understand the person's own evaluation, actual presentation, and situational pressures separately.
faq.question: Does stronger Modesty mean low self-esteem?

faq.answer: No. Check accuracy, relevance, and proportional credit. A portfolio review or handover may require an explicit account of personal responsibility. Volunteering that information alone does not decide whether the presentation was excessive.
faq.question: Is talking about an achievement necessarily boasting?

faq.answer: Name the task, your actions, relevant evidence, and collaborators' roles. Avoid both minimizing documented responsibility and claiming the entire shared result. Help the interviewer understand the evidence rather than trying to perform a trait label.
faq.question: How can I describe my work in an interview?

faq.answer: Yes, as one explanation to examine. Compare similar discussions across actual settings and note your expectations about reactions. Nationality, a polite phrase, or one quiet conversation cannot establish a stable tendency.
faq.question: Could my reserve reflect local expectations?

faq.answer: No. Capability requires evidence from relevant tasks and performance. A facet description or a short record of contribution discussions cannot replace that evidence.
faq.question: Can Modesty tell me how capable I am?

not_for: Do not use this page for clinical diagnosis or as the sole basis for hiring or admission.
method_boundary.summary: Use this page to understand personality concepts and examine everyday behavior. Interpret actual scores using the instrument’s scoring method, reference sample, and intended use.

sections.body:
Modesty concerns how someone views and emphasizes personal importance, status, achievements, or superiority. In the NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary used on this site, it belongs to Agreeableness. Everyday humility can also refer to moral ideals or ways of living; this page explains a personality facet rather than grading those ideals.

It is too narrow to define it solely as public presentation. The [official IPIP ten-item version](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOFacetsKey.htm) includes reluctance to discuss oneself or seek attention, views of one's own standing, and self-praise. The [Maples four-item version](https://ipip.ori.org/30FacetNEO-PI-RItems_Maples_etal.htm) samples self-superiority, high self-opinion, and becoming the center of attention; it does not reproduce every item from the longer version. These are descriptions of specific IPIP scales, not a statement of which items this site's assessment uses.

A stronger tendency may involve less emphasis on personal distinction. A weaker tendency may involve more emphasis on one's standing or recognition. Neither establishes whether an achievement is real, a skill is strong, or a person deserves admiration. These are continuous tendencies; a middle position is not a special type that automatically combines reserve with effective self-promotion.
sections.heading: More than a preference to stay quiet

sections.body:
Overall self-esteem concerns a person's evaluation of their worth. Competence requires evidence from relevant tasks. Self-presentation concerns what they communicate about themselves in a setting. These questions can be related, but they cannot substitute for one another.

Someone can acknowledge doing difficult work without presenting it as proof of superiority. Someone else can repeatedly mention achievements while privately doubting their worth. The latter interpretation needs the person's account or other suitable evidence; visible self-promotion alone cannot establish it.

Reserve does not prove a lack of expertise, and confident presentation does not prove expertise. If you need to know whether someone can do a job, examine relevant work and performance. Likewise, silence may reflect discomfort, a lack of opportunity, or a preference not to stand out. Do not select a motive from the silence itself.
sections.heading: Separate worth, competence, and what was said

sections.body:
A portfolio review may require an exact account of personal responsibility. A celebration may invite shared recognition. Saying “we” can accurately describe joint work or hide an important individual role; saying “I” can accurately name responsibility or omit collaborators. The pronoun does not decide the interpretation.

Teams and social groups differ in their expectations about praise and visibility. Check the actual setting rather than assigning a person the conventions associated with their nationality. Ask what information the audience needed and what consequences the speaker anticipated.

Rejecting every compliment, minimizing real work, or remaining silent is not a universal ideal. Accurate credit is a more useful communication goal than trying to appear maximally modest.
sections.heading: The audience changes the task

sections.body:
Accurately naming a contribution while making no claim to superiority is compatible with Modesty. Understating real work is not a required sign of stronger Modesty. The following example examines a possible communication habit; it is not a model of how a modest person ought to speak.

Try a focused hypothesis: “When peers ask about my contribution to a finished project, I usually describe my role as smaller than the project records show.”

In an invented example, Jordan created the sound design for a short film while another collaborator edited it. In several peer discussions, Jordan describes the work as “a little help with audio” and leaves out the sound-design responsibility. The credits and files support the observation that the role was minimized. They do not establish the motive: reserve, fear of appearing boastful, group conventions, and difficulty describing the work remain alternatives.

A natural counterexample occurs in another ordinary peer discussion, without a credit dispute or a prepared script, when Jordan accurately states the sound-design role and acknowledges the editor. The same opportunity existed, but minimization did not occur. One event can coexist with “usually”; recurring comparable examples should change the explanation.

A gathering where nobody asks about the project is not an opportunity of the same kind. Correcting a mistaken credit is worth recording too, but it has a different immediate task from a routine portfolio discussion.
sections.heading: A portfolio example that can be challenged

sections.body:
For natural contribution discussions, record the question, the documented division of work, the actual description, and constraints such as time or audience expectations. Record your own thoughts separately if you noticed them. Without that information, do not infer self-worth from wording.

Distinguish an opportunity with minimization, an opportunity without it, and no comparable opportunity. Having found no counterexample is an information gap, not proof that there are none. Posting little online or producing excellent work does not replace evidence about this target behavior.

Retain the local hypothesis provisionally if comparable discussions repeatedly show minimization and alternatives remain insufficient. Narrow it if the pattern appears only with one audience. Set it aside if the role or wording is unclear. Revise it if repeated opportunities produce accurate accounts. This exercise can clarify a communication habit; it cannot validate a trait or measure self-esteem.
sections.heading: Observe a pattern without turning it into a verdict

sections.body:
For a deliberate practice attempt, choose a safe occasion where the audience needs to know your role. Prepare what you did, the evidence, and what collaborators did. For example: “I designed and mixed the audio; these files show the revisions. Morgan handled the edit.” The aim is accurate information, not a more impressive persona.

Check whether the listener can identify the division of work and whether you omitted or inflated anyone's contribution. Their praise is not the sole success criterion, and a lack of praise does not assess your worth.

Mark this as prepared practice and keep it separate from natural discussions. If your concern is repeatedly redirecting conversations toward yourself, first identify the audience's actual question and give only the relevant account. Neither a prepared description nor a deliberate pause demonstrates personality change.

Keep a format that makes responsibility clearer. If it repeatedly confuses the listener or leaves an inaccurate account, revise the wording or choose a more suitable occasion. You can stop an unhelpful exercise while keeping useful notes or other support. Completing the introduction does not show that you felt confident or comfortable; record those experiences separately if they matter to your question.
sections.heading: Make one contribution legible

sections.body:
The [IPIP comparison table](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEO_FacetsTable.htm) places Modesty alongside NEO Modesty as a similar construct, not an interchangeable instrument. The 30-facet vocabulary belongs to this NEO/IPIP-NEO tradition; other Big Five tools use different structures. For example, the [BFI-2 authors' description](https://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~johnlab/bfi.html) specifies 15 facets.

You may also meet the name in another model. The [HEXACO authors' scale descriptions](https://hexaco.org/scaledescriptions) place Modesty under Honesty-Humility and describe one's view of superiority and entitlement to special treatment. This page follows the NEO/IPIP-NEO Agreeableness vocabulary. A shared name does not make scores, items, or interpretation rules transferable between models.

This page does not establish a separately measured Modesty result. Check the assessment's actual outputs and score explanation rather than deriving the facet from a domain score or assuming a percentage is a percentile. A percentile needs an identified reference population; a scale's percentage range alone does not provide that comparison.

Read [Agreeableness](/en/personality/big-five/agreeableness) for the broader dimension and the [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets) for the descriptive structure. For whether communication is truthful or misleading, continue with [Straightforwardness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/straightforwardness); the question here is how you view and emphasize your own standing. For your response to disagreement, see [Compliance](/en/personality/big-five/facets/compliance). Describing your contribution accurately does not by itself answer either neighboring question.

seo.description: Big Five Modesty concerns self-importance and self-presentation. Learn how it differs from self-esteem and how to describe achievements without distorting credit.

personality_public_content_asset_v1.summary: Modesty concerns your view of your own importance and how you present it. In the NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary, it is an Agreeableness facet. Accurate acknowledgment of an achievement can coexist with little desire to claim superiority.
